sections.h2: How can a Troy homeowner sell without months of showings?
sections.html:
The quick routes in Troy are an as-is cash purchase or a listing priced to move, and the better one depends on what the house needs. Troy has a mix of old brick homes near downtown and newer subdivisions, so repair needs vary widely from one address to the next.

  • Listing with an agent: good exposure across the Dayton region, with a buyer inspection and financing steps before closing.
  • Owner-handled sale: you write the contract, deliver the disclosure form and arrange the deed.
  • Direct as-is purchase: the buyer takes the house with its repairs, and closing can be scheduled around your move.

Whichever you pick, the deed has to clear the Miami County Auditor and Engineer before the Recorder files it.

sections.h2: What is Troy, Ohio like for a seller?
sections.html:
Troy is the county seat of Miami County and the county's largest city, on the Great Miami River about 19 miles north of Dayton. It was platted around 1807, and a post office has operated here since 1824. The Great Flood of 1913 hit the city hard, and the Great Miami River still shapes parts of the map. The city covers 11.94 square miles, 11.72 of them land.

Historic buildings give Troy a recognizable core. The 1808 Overfield Tavern is now a museum, the Troy-Hayner Cultural Center occupies a 1914 Romanesque mansion, and the Hobart Welded Steel House Company built 22 prefabricated houses, all in Troy, 16 of which survive and are listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Hobart Institute of Welding Technology has been here since 1930. The Troy Public Square and the Miami County Courthouse are also listed.

The city's Historic District is an overlay generally bounded by the Miami River on the north, Clay Street on the east, Canal Street on the south and Oxford Street on the west. The Planning Commission reviews alterations to properties inside it, so owners of historic houses should check before planning exterior changes ahead of a sale.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers show for Troy?
sections.html:
Troy is one of the few Ohio cities in this group that grew: the July 1, 2025 estimate is 27,344 residents, up 3.8 percent from the April 2020 base. Troy has gained population in every census since 1990.

sections.h2: Which Troy schools do buyers look at?
sections.html:
Troy City Schools serves most of the city, with Troy High School for grades 9 to 12 and Troy Junior High for grades 7 and 8. Public elementary schools are Concord, Cookson, Forest, Heywood, Hook, Kyle and Van Cleve. Part of the city lies in the Miami East Local School District, so confirm a specific address before advertising a school assignment.

Private options include Troy Christian (Pre-K to 12), St. Patrick School for kindergarten to 8 and Miami Montessori School. The Troy-Miami County Public Library has three locations in the city.

sections.h2: How do Troy's property maintenance and zoning rules affect a sale?
sections.html:
Troy has adopted the International Property Maintenance Code for existing homes and other structures, and violations can lead to penalties imposed by the courts. City staff respond to complaints and also spot problems on their own. A checklist for judging the exterior condition of a property is published by the city, and using it before listing is a cheap way to find peeling paint, broken steps or overgrown lots.

The Planning and Zoning Division issues zoning permits and administers the city's Unified Development Code, which sets setbacks and permitted uses. If you added a shed, deck or pool, make sure the permit was closed out. Permit filing runs through the city's online portal.

sections.h2: What does Troy require about water service lines and utilities?
sections.html:
Homes in Troy built before February 1, 1944 may have lead water service lines. Under the EPA's Lead and Copper Rule the city is inventorying service line materials, and owners of those older homes receive a yearly letter until the line is replaced or the material is verified. Options are a 15-minute inspection by a city technician, available Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. by calling 937-335-4151, or a self-report through the city's online form.

For the buyer's side, the Utility Billing office needs a deed, closing papers or the accepted purchase contract, and photo ID, to open service in an owner's name. It also asks that any delinquency be settled before new service starts, so clear your account and arrange a final reading around the closing date. The office is at City Hall, 100 S. Market Street.

sections.h2: How does a Troy deed move through Miami County?
sections.html:
Miami County's conveyance standards, adopted August 12, 2025, set the order. The County Engineer's office approves the instrument first. The Auditor then needs the completed DTE 100 statement of value or the DTE 100 EX exemption form, and the Recorder files the deed once it carries the Auditor and Engineer approval stamps.

  • The grantor on the deed must match the prior grantee, or an affidavit under Ohio Revised Code 5301.252 must explain a break in the chain of title.
  • Land contracts must be approved by the Engineer and date-stamped by the Auditor before recording.
  • Checks for the conveyance fee must match the exact amount and be payable to the Miami County Auditor, since overpayments are refused.
  • The auditor's website has a conveyance fee calculator that includes the parcel transfer fee.

The county transfer tax falls on the grantor under Ohio Revised Code 322.02. Next-of-kin affidavits, survivorship transfers and transfer on death designations follow separate steps under the same standards, which matters for inherited Troy houses.

sections.h2: What does the Ohio disclosure statute say about timing?
sections.html:
Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 sets a rescission window for buyers. If a buyer first receives the property disclosure form after signing, the buyer can rescind in writing within three business days of receipt, and cannot do so after 30 days from acceptance or the closing, whichever comes first. A buyer who gets the form before making an offer has no such right.

Give the form to prospective buyers at the start. Troy sellers who inherited the house and did not live there in the prior year are exempt.

faqs.q: Where do I file a deed for a Troy house?
faqs.a: Troy is the Miami County seat, so a deed goes through the County Engineer, the County Auditor and the County Recorder. Start with the Engineer's approval, then the Auditor's conveyance forms.

faqs.q: Does Troy have a historic district that limits changes?
faqs.a: Yes. The Historic District overlay runs between the Miami River, Clay Street, Canal Street and Oxford Street, and the Planning Commission reviews alterations. Ask Planning and Zoning whether your address is inside it.

faqs.q: Will an old Troy home need a lead service line inspection?
faqs.a: Homes built before February 1, 1944 are in the city's inventory. Owners get an annual letter until the line is replaced or its material is confirmed through a city inspection or an online self-report.

faqs.q: Who pays the conveyance fee when a Troy house sells?
faqs.a: The seller, as grantor, under Ohio Revised Code 322.02. The Miami County Auditor's site has a calculator that includes the parcel transfer fee, so use it with your sale price before closing.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Troy house with unpermitted work?
faqs.a: You can, but the buyer's inspector may ask for permits. Contact Planning and Zoning about any shed, deck or pool, and consider fixing or documenting it before listing.
